MINUTES OF THE MORNING SESSION
WEDNESDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1933
Old Chapel, Union College, Schenectady, New York
'T'HE Convention was called to order at 11:00 A. M. in the Old Chapel of
Union College, Schenectady, New York, by Edward L. Stevens, Chi '99,
senior degelate of the Executive Council. Brother Stevens appointed the
following temporary officers:
Temporary President�
George R. Cory, Jr., Theta '34
Temporary Recorder�
Harold E. EUithom, Theta '34
Brother George Cory, as Temporary President, took the chair and
extended the official welcome of the Theta to the delegates to the Centennial
Convention. He also expressed the sincere appreciation of the Theta to the
Centennial Committee for its splendid work in preparing the Centennial
program.
The Temporary President then appointed the following Committees:

At the end of the recess the Convention was called to order by the Tem
porary President George Cory at 11:20 A. M.

On motion duly made, seconded and passed this report was accepted
unanimously. The Temporary Recorder was instructed to cast one baUot
for the election of the permanent officers nominated, inasmuch as no other
nominations were presented.
President Edward L. Stevens, Chi '99 was escorted to the Chair; He
thanked the delegates for the honor conferred upon him of presiding over the
Centennial Convention; he then welcomed the delegates to the Centennial
Convention.
The Annual Communication of the Executive Council was then read by
its Secretary, R. Bourke Corcoran, Omega '15 (See Appendix "A").
On motion duly made, seconded and passed this communication was
accepted and placed on file.
The Annual Report of the Treasurer of the Executive Council was read;
by R. Bourke Corcoran, Omega '15 in the absence from this session of the
Treasurer, Kenneth A. O'Brien, Sigma '28 (See Appendix "B").
Brother Charles P. Spooner, Rho '94, a member of the Executive
Council made a brief statement explaining the modest income and expenditures
of our Council ; he said that the national dues of our undergraduates were the
lowest of any fraternity ($4.00 per year per man) and this was made possible
by the fact that the officers and members of the Executive Council gave their
services whereas in aU other fraternities we know about they have one to a
number of members who received regular salaries.
On motion duly made, seconded and passed, the report of the Treasurer
was accepted and placed on file.
The Convention Rules of Psi Upsilon as adopted April 7th, 1892 and as
amended in 1909 were then read by the Secretary of the Executive Cotmcil
R. Bourke Corcoran, Omega 'IS. President Stevens then suggested that
these rules be amended as follows:

Old Chapel, Union College, Schenectady, New York

MINUTES OF THE MEETING OF THE COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
WEDNESDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1933
Brother Charles P. Spooner caUed the meeting to order at 3 :30 P. M.
Brother Corcoran introduced Mr. Corbett, representative of the Wrang
lers, who presented such data and information as he felt would support the
Wranglers fitness for a charter from Psi Upsilon. FoUowing his address he
answered a number of questions which were asked by a number of members of
the Committee. He then withdrew.
Brother Spooner related the experiences of the Rho Kappa Upsilon
Society many years before in their effort to secure a charter, which ended in
the estabUshment of our present Rho Chapter.
Brother Corcoran then presented Mr. C. J. Armstrong representing
Alpha Kappa Alpha. Mr. Armstrong gave such information and data in his
address concerning his Society and the University of British Columbia as he
felt would support their petition for a charter. He also answered a number
of questions which were asked by members of the Committee. He then
withdrew.
On motion duly made, seconded and passed, it was voted to reconvene
the Executive Session of the Convention.
AFTERNOON SESSION (Continued)
President Stevens took the Chair and caUed the meeting to order at
4:35 P. M.
The session was then opened for an informal discussion of the petitions,
as the Committee on New Business had not, as yet, held a meeting to present
their recommendations.
Discussion both favorable and unfavorable on these two petitions followed.
The Secretary of the Executive Council read a telegram of greeting from
Brother Eari D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93; also a letter from Brother Ralph W. C.
ShuU, Mu '09 of Beverly Hills, Cahfornia, regarding the status of the Uni
versity of Cahfornia, Los Angeles Branch for a prospective charter of our
Fraternity. The latter was referred to the Committee on New Business.
It was moved, seconded and voted to adjourn until Thursday morning,
November 23 at 10:00 A. M.

Robert E. Langford, Omega '34:
We, the Committee hereby present the following resolutions:
No. I. Resolved: That this Convention held in the 100th year of
Psi Upsilon, extends its hearty thanks to the Theta Chapter, its alumni

for their cordial hospitality and thoughtful consideration to the plans

No. 2. Resolved: That the place, date and other details of the next
year's Convention be left to the Executive Council with power.
No. 3. Resolved: That greetings of the Convention be sent to:
Dr. George Henry Fox, Upsilon '67, Honorary President of the
Executive Council, who is ill.
Mrs. WiUiam Howard Taft.
Mrs. Herbert Lawrence Bridgman and to others selected by the
Executive Council.
No. 4. Resolved: That the petition of the Alpha Kappa Alpha
Society at the University of British Columbia be referred to the Chapters
in Psi Upsilon for a vote.
No. 5. Resolved: That the petition of the Wranglers at North
western University be referred to the various Chapters in Psi Upsilon
for a vote.
On motion duly made, seconded and passed the report was accepted.

It was duly moved, seconded and voted to send a message of sympathy

Announcements were then made concerning the remainder of the Cen

Respectfully submitted,

Appendix A
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
OF THE
EXECUTIVE COUNCIL OF PSI UPSILON
TO THE 1933 CONVENTION OF THE FRATERNITY
HELD WITH THE THETA CHAPTER
NOVEMBER 22 AND 23, 1933
IN CONNECTION WITH THE CENTENNIAL CELEBRATION OF
THE FRATERNITY HELD ON NOVEMBER 24, 1933.
This Convention of Psi Upsilon is unique in the Fraternity's annals, in
that it is held in November rather than in the Spring and will lead up to and
merge into our Centennial Celebration on November 24th. All other conven
tions, while attended by many of our alumni, seem of less importance com
pared to this one which brings together more undergraduates and alumni
than any in our history and prepares for the fitting celebration of the end of
the first century of Psi Upsilon's existence. During that long period since the
inauguration of annual conventions, only two years have passed without a
meeting of the delegates from the undergraduate chapters, 1842 and 1917.
It will be for this Convention to determine whether we will resume the
normal course of Spring Conventions in 1934 or wiU make some other disposi
tion of our annual meetings. At the present time the Beta Beta Chapter is
ready to accept this Convention ; should it not be a short two day gathering
with but one delegate from each Chapter, in view of economic conditions,
rather than to allow a year to lapse?
Vote on Petition: By resolution of the 1932 Convention, the petitions
of "The Wranglers"of Northwestern University and of the Alpha Kappa Alpha
Fraternity of the University of British Columbia were submitted to the
Chapters of our Fraternity for appropriate action, with the instruction that
such action be taken and reported to the Executive Cotmcil before the close
of the current college year. The result of the action of the Chapters on these
petitions was as follows:
"The Wranglers" petition�
^favorable 16; unfavorable 10; not voting 1.
Alpha Kappa Alpha petition�
favorable 18; unfavorable 8; not voting 1.
It seems to the Executive Cotmcil that perhaps our Chapters, in consider
ing petitions for Psi UpsUon Charters, are overlooking one vitally essential
matter, that is that the basis for the choice of a new chapter is the same,
fundamentaUy, as the basis for the choice of members of a chapter. It must
be remembered that the granting of a charter to a group of petitioners evenPage Thirteen

PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
prior to the Centennial over 2700 changes of addresses were received by us
and in the last issue of the "Diamond" we
pubHshed a list of approximately
650 Brothers for whom we had no correct address.
We cannot impress too strongly upon the Chapters the necessity of main
taining an accurate list of their own alumni and of co-operating with the
Alumni Association and the Executive Council in this regard.
The Diamond: Since the last Convention of the Fraternity seven issues
of the "Diamond" have been sent out; the November 1933 issue being sent
to aU members of the Fraternity. We are pleased to state that the cost of
pubhshing these issues, together with the other expenses of the "Diamond",
has been $333.84 under the income received for the "Diamond". This
has been made possible through curtailing the size of the issues and
the number of inserts and cuts used. Likewise, we have omitted from the
January and June numbers of each year the Chapter Communications purely
as a matter of economy. The facts are that the surplus remaining from the
cost of publishing the "Diamond" since the last Convention is greater than
indicated in the Treasurer's report, due to the fact that coUections from the
Chapters of their "Diamond" subscription fees between November 1st and
the time of the Convention amount to over
$700., which wiU be available for
future years. In addition to the cost of pubUshing the magazine, the "Dia
mond" bears one-third of the expense of maintaining the headquarters office
of the Fraternity and a hke portion of the salary of the stenographer in the
office.
The editor of the "Diamond", Brother Corcoran, has just resigned,
having published aU numbers of the "Diamond" since its revival in 1920.
He bespeaks the continued co-operation of the Chapters and Alumni Associa
tion for his successor in this labor of love.
The Centennial: In view of the fact that we are now in the home of
our Mother Chapter and in the atmosphere of the Centennial Celebration,
which wiU take place throughout the day and evening of November 24 now
only two days away, and that the whole Fraternity, through the medimn of
the latest issue of the "Diamond", has been informed of the details of this One
Hundredth Anniversary of Founders Day, it is unnecessary to go into it
further at this time. The co-operation of the new Alumni Association of Psi
Upsilon, of the Theta and its Centennial Committee, of the members of the
General Centennial Committee of the Fraternity and of aU of our alumni
upon whom we have caUed, in preparing for this great event, is gratefully
acknowledged by the Council.

dent and a Temporary Recorder.
II

1. A Committee on Credentials.
2. A Committee on Permanent Organization.
Ill
The permanent officers shaU be a President, three or more Vice-Presidents,
a Recorder, and two Assistant Recorders.
IV
The Recorder and his Assistants shaU record the proceedings of the
Convention, and within twenty-four hours after the final adjournment shall
transmit to the Executive Council the record and aU papers relating to the
business of the Convention.
V
When the permanent officers shaU have been chosen, the Annual Com
munication of the Executive Council shall be read. The President shall then
appoint standing committees of four or more members each, as follows:
1. The Committee to nominate members of the Executive CouncU.
2. The Committee on the Annual Communication, which shall consider
and report upon the matters embraced in the Annual Communication.
3. The Committee on Unfinished Business, which shaU consider and
report upon aU measures considered, but not finally determined, by the
previous Convention, excepting such matters as shall have been referred to
the Committee on the Annual Communication.
4. The Committee on New Business, which shaU consider and report
upon aU new petitions or new business of any kind presented to the Convention.
